claim: The evolution of multicellularity is a major transition in individuality, from autonomously replicating cells to groups of interdependent cells forming a higher-level of organisation.
source: The evolution of multicellularity is a major transition in individuality, from autonomously replicating cells to groups of interdependent cells forming a higher-level of organisation (Buss, 2014; Smith and Szathmary, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buss, 2014 and Smith and Szathmary, 1995

claim: Multicellularity has evolved independently several times across the tree of life.
source: It has evolved independently several times across the tree of life (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007; Parfrey and Lahr, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007 and Parfrey and Lahr, 2013

claim: Comparative genomics suggests that the increase of cell–cell adhesion drives the early evolution of undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: Comparative genomics suggests (Knoll, 2011), and experimental evolution confirms (Boraas et al., 1998; Ratcliff et al., 2012) that the increase of cell–cell adhesion drives the early evolution of (undifferentiated) multicellularity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Knoll, 2011 for comparative genomics

claim: Experimental evolution confirms that the increase of cell–cell adhesion drives the early evolution of undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: Comparative genomics suggests (Knoll, 2011), and experimental evolution confirms (Boraas et al., 1998; Ratcliff et al., 2012) that the increase of cell–cell adhesion drives the early evolution of (undifferentiated) multicellularity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Boraas et al., 1998 and Ratcliff et al., 2012 for experimental evolution

claim: Increased cell adhesion may be temporally limited and/or may be triggered by environmental changes in Dictyostelids and Myxobacteria.
source: Increased cell adhesion may be temporally limited and/or may be triggered by environmental changes (e.g. in Dictyostelids and Myxobacteria [Du et al., 2015; Kaiser et al., 1979]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Du et al., 2015 and Kaiser et al., 1979

claim: Multicellular organisation may come about either by aggregation of genetically distinct cells or by incomplete separation after cell division.
source: Moreover, multicellular organisation may come about either by aggregation of genetically distinct cells or by incomplete separation after cell division (King, 2004; Du et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to King, 2004 and Du et al., 2015

claim: The genetic toolkit and cellular components that allow for multicellularity pre-date multicellular species and are found in their unicellular relatives.
source: The genetic toolkit and the cellular components that allow for multicellularity - including adhesion proteins - pre-date multicellular species and are found in their unicellular relatives (Rokas, 2008; Prochnik et al., 2010; Du et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rokas, 2008; Prochnik et al., 2010; Du et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2018

claim: The formation of early multicellular groups has been studied in the context of the evolution of cooperation by incorporating game theoretical interactions and transient compartimentalisation.
source: The formation of early multicellular groups has been studied in the context of the evolution of cooperation: by incorporating game theoretical interactions and transient compartimentalisation (Garcia et al., 2014) or the possibility of differential assortment (Joshi et al., 2017), it was found that adhering groups of cooperating individuals evolve.
evidence: Supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2014

claim: Adhering groups of cooperating individuals evolve when the possibility of differential assortment is included.
source: The formation of early multicellular groups has been studied in the context of the evolution of cooperation: by incorporating game theoretical interactions and transient compartimentalisation (Garcia et al., 2014) or the possibility of differential assortment (Joshi et al., 2017), it was found that adhering groups of cooperating individuals evolve.
evidence: Supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2017

claim: Reproductive trade-offs can give rise to division of labour.
source: Alternatively, reproductive trade-offs can give rise to division of labour (Solari et al., 2013) and lead to the formation of a higher-level proto-organism capable of self-regeneration in a structured environment (Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solari et al., 2013

claim: Reproductive trade-offs lead to the formation of a higher-level proto-organism capable of self-regeneration in a structured environment.
source: Alternatively, reproductive trade-offs can give rise to division of labour (Solari et al., 2013) and lead to the formation of a higher-level proto-organism capable of self-regeneration in a structured environment (Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016

claim: A plethora of multicellular life-cycles can emerge by simple considerations about the ecology of the uni-cellular ancestor and the fitness benefit that cells acquire by being in groups.
source: A plethora of multicellular life-cycles can emerge by simple considerations about the ecology of the uni-cellular ancestor and the fitness benefit that cells acquire by being in groups (Staps et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Staps et al., 2019

claim: The spatial organisation of cells in multicellular clusters can play an important role in determining group-level reproduction, possibly leading to the evolution of cell-death.
source: Once multicellular clusters are established, the spatial organisation of their composing cells can play an important role in determining group-level reproduction - possibly leading to the evolution of cell-death (Libby et al., 2014) or different cell shapes (Jacobeen et al., 2018), and to specific modes of fragmentation of the aggregate (Pichugin et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019) that increase overall population growth.
evidence: Supported by citation to Libby et al., 2014

claim: The spatial organisation of cells in multicellular clusters can lead to the evolution of different cell shapes.
source: Once multicellular clusters are established, the spatial organisation of their composing cells can play an important role in determining group-level reproduction - possibly leading to the evolution of cell-death (Libby et al., 2014) or different cell shapes (Jacobeen et al., 2018), and to specific modes of fragmentation of the aggregate (Pichugin et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019) that increase overall population growth.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobeen et al., 2018

claim: The spatial organisation of cells in multicellular clusters can lead to specific modes of fragmentation of the aggregate that increase overall population growth.
source: Once multicellular clusters are established, the spatial organisation of their composing cells can play an important role in determining group-level reproduction - possibly leading to the evolution of cell-death (Libby et al., 2014) or different cell shapes (Jacobeen et al., 2018), and to specific modes of fragmentation of the aggregate (Pichugin et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019) that increase overall population growth.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pichugin et al., 2017 and Gao et al., 2019

claim: Previous models have shown how cell collectives are able to integrate noisy information from the environment when moving up a shallow chemoattractant gradient.
source: Previous models have shown how cell collectives are able to integrate noisy information from the environment, for instance when moving up a shallow chemoattractant gradient. (Marée et al., 1999; Szabó et al., 2006; Kabla, 2012; Szabó et al., 2010; Camley and Rappel, 2017; George et al., 2017; Camley, 2018; Varennes et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous modeling work

claim: The Cellular Potts Model formalism is a spatially extended, mesoscopic description of cells which explicitly accounts for cell shape and size.
source: The CPM formalism is a spatially extended, mesoscopic description of cells which explicitly accounts for cell shape and size, and allows for a straightforward implementation various cellular processes within complex and potentially self-organised environments.
evidence: This is a description of the CPM model used in the study, based on established knowledge of the method

claim: Individual cells follow the chemotactic signal very inefficiently in a noisy and shallow gradient.
source: Because the gradient generated by the resources is noisy and shallow, we find that individual cells follow the chemotactic signal very inefficiently.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations described in the manuscript

claim: Cells that adhere to each other within groups transfer information about the gradient in a self-organised manner, allowing for efficient chemotaxis.
source: Instead, cells that adhere to each other within groups transfer information about the gradient in a self-organised manner, allowing for efficient chemotaxis in our model.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations described in the manuscript

claim: For longer seasons, the emergent property of cell groups performing efficient chemotaxis is sufficient to select for high levels of adhesion and multicellularity.
source: We show that for longer seasons, this emergent property of cell groups is sufficient to select for high levels of adhesion and multicellularity, despite the fact that fitness is only defined at the cell level.
evidence: This is a main finding from the evolutionary simulations in the manuscript

claim: The CPM formalism captures the fact that biological cells are dissipative objects with deformable boundaries.
source: The CPM formalism captures the fact that biological cells are dissipative objects with deformable boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of what the CPM model represents, based on established knowledge

claim: Cell movement arises from stochastic fluctuations (extensions and retractions) of the cell boundaries.
source: Cell movement arises from stochastic fluctuations (extensions and retractions) of the cell boundaries.
evidence: This describes how cell movement is implemented in the CPM model

claim: Adhesion strength increases linearly with the number of complementary bits in the ligand and receptor.
source: Adhesion strength increases linearly with the number of complementary bits in the ligand and receptor.
evidence: This describes how adhesion is calculated in the model

claim: Persistent migration occurs through biasing cell membrane fluctuations towards the previous direction of motion of a cell.
source: Following (Beltman et al., 2007), persistent migration occurs through biasing cell membrane fluctuations towards the previous direction of motion of a cell (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the implementation of persistent migration, citing Beltman et al., 2007 and referencing Figure 1b

claim: Eukaryotic cells repeatedly reorient the polymerisation of the actin cytoskeleton during chemotaxis, which takes some time, resulting in a migration pattern that is persistent over short time scales.
source: During chemotaxis, eukaryotic cells repeatedly reorient the polymerisation of the actin cytoskeleton. This reorientation takes some time (Ridley et al., 2003), resulting in a migration pattern that is persistent over short time scales.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ridley et al., 2003

claim: The chemoattractant is released at low concentration by resources present at one end of the grid, creating a shallow and noisy gradient over the grid.
source: We assume that this chemoattractant is released at low concentration by resources present at one end of the grid, creating a shallow and noisy gradient over the grid (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the model setup, with reference to Figure 1c

claim: The division probability is inversely proportional to the distance of the cell to the gradient peak.
source: To reflect the assumption that more nutrients are present at higher concentrations of the signal, the division probability is inversely proportional to the distance of the cell to the gradient peak and cells very close to the gradient peak may divide multiple times.
evidence: This describes how fitness is calculated in the model

claim: Daughter cells inherit mutated copies of the ligand and receptor, so that their adhesive properties can change with respect to the parent.
source: The daughter cells inherit mutated copies of the ligand and receptor, so that their adhesive properties can change with respect to the parent.
evidence: This describes the mutation mechanism in the evolutionary model

claim: Related cells remain close at the beginning of the new season because cell dispersal after replication is not included.
source: Note that we do not include cell dispersal after replication, therefore related cells remain close at the beginning of the new season.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model setup

claim: Multicellularity is not selected for directly: the fitness function rewards cells for their proximity to resources without explicitly incorporating a fitness advantage or disadvantage for the multicellular state.
source: We do not select for multicellularity directly: the fitness function rewards cells for their proximity to resources, and we do not explicitly incorporate a fitness advantage or disadvantage for the multicellular state.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model design

claim: Multicellular clusters can arise only because they perform an emergent task that single cells cannot perform.
source: Therefore, multicellular clusters (Figure 2a,c,d) can arise only because they perform an emergent task that single cells cannot perform.
evidence: This is an inference from the model design, with reference to Figure 2

claim: Non-adhering cells tend to lose contact from one another during chemotaxis.
source: Chemotaxis is inefficient, because these cells tend to lose contact from one another (Video 3) and once isolated they behave like those from simulations with one cell (Figure 3a,b 'one cell').
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Video 3 and Figure 3a,b

claim: Single cells show large variance between different simulations in their chemotaxis performance.
source: Single cells also show large variance between different simulations (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Figure 3b

claim: In a non-adhering population some cells reach the peak of the gradient almost as quickly as an adhering cluster does.
source: Thus, in a non-adhering population some cells reach the peak of the gradient almost as quickly as an adhering cluster does.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results

claim: The speed of the cell closest to the peak of the gradient is roughly the same regardless of adhesion strength.
source: While cell clusters perform chemotaxis efficiently only when cells adhere, the speed of the cell closest to the peak of the gradient is roughly the same regardless of adhesion strength (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Figure 3b

claim: The MSD of a single cell is approximately linear and its diffusive exponent tends to 1, indicating that cells' movement is much more dominated by diffusion.
source: Instead, the MSD of a single cell (Figure 3c, one cell) is approximately linear and its diffusive exponent tends to 1, indicating that cells' movement is much more dominated by diffusion.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Figure 3c

claim: There is no difference in the instantaneous speed of cells when they are in a cluster or when they are alone.
source: Interestingly, there is no difference in the instantaneous speed of cells when they are in a cluster or when they are alone (Figure 3e), so the higher rate of displacement of a group of adhering cells is only due to larger persistence in the direction of motion.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Figure 3e

claim: The higher rate of displacement of a group of adhering cells is only due to larger persistence in the direction of motion.
source: Interestingly, there is no difference in the instantaneous speed of cells when they are in a cluster or when they are alone (Figure 3e), so the higher rate of displacement of a group of adhering cells is only due to larger persistence in the direction of motion.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results

claim: Although the cluster moves straight towards the source of the gradient, individual cells follow noisy trajectories.
source: Although the cluster moves straight towards the source of the gradient, individual cells follow noisy trajectories.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, also shown in Figure 4

claim: Cluster speed saturates quickly with the number of cells, at a smaller speed than that of individual cells.
source: Instead, we found that cluster speed saturates quickly with the number of cells, at a smaller speed than that of individual cells (cf. Appendix 1.2 with Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Appendix 1.2 and Figure 3e

claim: Individual contributions to cluster chemotaxis are not simply averaged.
source: We conclude that individual contributions to cluster chemotaxis are not simply averaged.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results

claim: Through persistent migration, a cell pushes other cells within an adhering cluster, and is pushed by them.
source: Through persistent migration, a cell pushes other cells within an adhering cluster, and is pushed by them.
evidence: This describes an emergent behavior observed in the simulations

claim: The resulting forces from persistent migration are resolved when cells align and form streams within the cluster.
source: The resulting forces are resolved when cells align and form streams within the cluster (see Video 4).
evidence: This describes an emergent behavior observed in the simulations, with reference to Video 4

claim: Through streaming, small clusters generate extensions, retractions and rotations, so that the entire cluster visually resembles a single amoeboid cell.
source: Through streaming, these small clusters generate extensions, retractions and rotations (Video 4), so that the entire cluster visually resembles a single amoeboid cell (Video 2).
evidence: This describes an emergent behavior observed in the simulations, with reference to Video 4 and Video 2

claim: The streaming behavior is not influenced by the presence of the chemotactic signal, since the flow field is identical when the chemotactic signal is removed.
source: This behaviour is not influenced by the presence of the chemotactic signal, since the flow field is identical when the chemotactic signal is removed (Appendix 1.3).
evidence: This is a finding from control simulations described in Appendix 1.3

claim: The effect of persistent migration is to align the direction of motion of the cells in a cluster.
source: Thus, the effect of persistent migration is to align the direction of motion of the cells in a cluster.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation observations

claim: Cell streams preferentially align towards the direction of the gradient, although aligning is not strictly required for chemotaxis.
source: This in turn speeds up collective chemotaxis, as cell streams preferentially align towards the direction of the gradient, although aligning is not strictly required for chemotaxis (Appendix 1.4).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Appendix 1.4

claim: Chemotactic migration improves with cell size because larger cells perceive a larger area of the chemotactic signal.
source: Because larger cells perceive a larger area of the chemotactic signal, chemotactic migration improves with cell size (Appendix 1.7).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations with different cell sizes, described in Appendix 1.7

claim: The measurements of individual cells deviate significantly from the true direction of the gradient.
source: We found that the measurements of individual cells deviate significantly from the true direction of the gradient (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations, with reference to Figure 3f

claim: Despite individual cells' measurements deviating from the true gradient direction, they are carried in the right direction by the other cells.
source: Despite this, they are carried in the right direction by the other cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations

claim: Cells in a cluster tend to migrate for longer in straight lines compared to single cells.
source: We find that cells in a cluster tend to migrate for longer in straight lines, and that these straight lines are also more likely to be oriented towards the source of the gradient (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is a finding from trajectory analysis, with reference to Figure 3g

claim: Straight line segments of cells in a cluster are more likely to be oriented towards the source of the gradient.
source: We find that cells in a cluster tend to migrate for longer in straight lines, and that these straight lines are also more likely to be oriented towards the source of the gradient (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is a finding from trajectory analysis, with reference to Figure 3g

claim: For single cells, there is no bias in the orientation of straight line segments towards the gradient source.
source: For single cells, there is no such bias.
evidence: This is a finding from trajectory analysis

claim: Cluster organisation emerges from cells altering each others' paths by exerting pushing and pulling forces through their persistent migration, which in turn results in efficient collective chemotaxis.
source: In conclusion, cluster organisation emerges from cells altering each others' paths by exerting pushing and pulling forces through their persistent migration, which in turn results in efficient collective chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion summarizing the mechanism of collective chemotaxis

claim: The emergence of reliable chemotactic behaviour in adhering cell clusters suggests an evolutionary path to multicellularity.
source: The emergence of reliable chemotactic behaviour in adhering cell clusters suggests an evolutionary path to multicellularity: a population of cells may aggregate if collective chemotaxis allows cells to find resources more reliably.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation results

claim: There are many factors that restrict cell size, such as the complexity of the metabolism and cellular mechanisms such as cell division.
source: While cells could improve their ability to sense the gradient individually by becoming bigger, there are many factors that restrict cell size, such as the complexity of the metabolism and cellular mechanisms such as cell division (Björklund and Marguerat, 2017; Marshall et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Björklund and Marguerat, 2017 and Marshall et al., 2012

claim: Cell size is assumed to be fixed in the evolutionary model, and cells evolve adhesion in response to a seasonally changing environment.
source: We therefore assume that cell size is fixed, and we let cells evolve adhesion - that is, the receptor and ligands expressed by the cells - in response to a seasonally changing environment, where the gradient is generated by a volatile resource that periodically changes position.
evidence: This describes the evolutionary model setup

claim: Cells closer to the peak of the gradient have a higher chance to reproduce at the end of the season.
source: Cells closer to the peak of the gradient have a higher chance to reproduce at the end of the season, and related cells remain close to each other at the beginning of the new season (there is no cell dispersal phase, see also model setup and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the fitness function in the evolutionary model

claim: At evolutionary steady state, all cells adhere strongly and with roughly the same energy to one another.
source: At evolutionary steady state, all cells adhere strongly and with roughly the same energy to one another (Appendix 2.1).
evidence: This is a finding from the evolutionary simulations, with reference to Appendix 2.1

claim: Although non-adhering cells follow the chemotactic signal only weakly, the spreading over the course of multiple seasons ensures that at least some cells end up close to the source of the gradient at the end of the season.
source: Although non-adhering cells follow the chemotactic signal only weakly, the spreading over the course of multiple seasons ensures that at least some cells end up close to the source of the gradient at the end of the season (Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the evolutionary simulations, with reference to Video 6

claim: A cluster of adhering cells is at disadvantage when seasons are short because it does not have enough time to reach the source of the chemotactic signal.
source: In contrast, a cluster of adhering cells is at disadvantage when seasons are short because it does not have enough time to reach the source of the chemotactic signal.
evidence: This is an explanation for the evolutionary outcome

claim: Over the course of multiple seasons, an adhering cluster ends up in the centre of the lattice and all its composing cells have the same (low) fitness.
source: Over the course of multiple seasons, an adhering cluster ends up in the centre of the lattice (Video 7) and all its composing cells have the same (low) fitness.
evidence: This is an observation from the evolutionary simulations, with reference to Video 7

claim: The connectedness of a cluster of adhering cells is locally disrupted when excess cells are culled between seasons.
source: Furthermore, the connectedness of a cluster of adhering cells is locally disrupted when excess cells are culled between seasons (Figure 2b), which briefly reduces the efficiency of collective migration.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations, with reference to Figure 2b

claim: Culling plays a minor role in the evolutionary outcome of the system because cells reconnect within 2000 MCS.
source: Because this phase is short-lived - cells reconnect within 2000 MCS - we expect that culling plays a minor role in the evolutionary outcome of the system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells reconnect quickly

claim: When seasons are sufficiently long, clusters of adhering cells have enough time to reach the source of the gradient.
source: When seasons are sufficiently long, clusters of adhering cells have enough time to reach the source of the gradient.
evidence: This is an explanation for the evolutionary outcome

claim: When seasons are sufficiently long, the fitness of cells within a cluster outweighs that of non-adhering cells, because clustering increases the chances of reaching the peak of the gradient.
source: At this point, the fitness of cells within a cluster outweighs that of non-adhering cells, because clustering increases the chances of reaching the peak of the gradient.
evidence: This is an explanation for the evolutionary outcome

claim: Results are robust to changes in gradient shape (assuming resources are located over an entire side of the lattice with straight isoclines).
source: Results are also robust to changes in gradient shape (assuming that resources are located over an entire side of the lattice, we tested a gradient with straight isoclines in Appendix 2.4) and to steeper, noiseless gradients (Appendix 2.5).
evidence: This is a finding from robustness tests described in Appendix 2.4

claim: Results are robust to steeper, noiseless gradients.
source: Results are also robust to changes in gradient shape (assuming that resources are located over an entire side of the lattice, we tested a gradient with straight isoclines in Appendix 2.4) and to steeper, noiseless gradients (Appendix 2.5).
evidence: This is a finding from robustness tests described in Appendix 2.5

claim: The evolution of multicellularity does not depend on the precise mechanism for collective chemotaxis.
source: Furthermore, the evolution of multicellularity does not depend on the precise mechanism for collective chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from robustness tests with alternative mechanisms

claim: Results are robust to an alternative model of collective chemotaxis that relies only on concentration sensing and contact inhibition of locomotion.
source: To show this, we relax the assumption that individual cells sense the gradient by implementing a recently proposed mechanism of emergent collective chemotaxis that relies only on concentration sensing (Camley et al., 2016). Following Camley et al., 2016, we assume that cell polarisation is inhibited at the sites of cell–cell contact (a phenomenon called contact inhibition of locomotion, see Mayor and Carmona-Fontaine, 2010 for a review), and that the magnitude of their polarisation is proportional to the concentration - not the gradient - of the chemoattractant. In Appendix 3.1, we show that results are robust to this modification of the chemotaxis mechanism.
evidence: This is a finding from robustness tests described in Appendix 3.1, citing Camley et al., 2016 and Mayor and Carmona-Fontaine, 2010

claim: The distance to the peak after 30×10³ MCS of a cluster of adhering cells is larger (i.e. their fitness is smaller) if they are hindered by a population of non-adhering cells in front of them.
source: The distance to the peak after 30 × 103 MCS of a cluster of adhering cells is larger (i.e. their fitness is smaller) if they are hindered by a population of non-adhering cells in front of them.
evidence: This is a finding from competition experiments

claim: There is interference competition (i.e. direct competition due to displacement) between populations of cells with different strategies.
source: Taken together, these results show that there is interference competition (i.e. direct competition due to displacement) between populations of cells with different strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the competition experiments

claim: In the evolutionary experiments, mutants with a slightly different strategy are generated during reproduction at the end of each season and interference competition continually prevents their successful invasion for intermediate season duration.
source: In the evolutionary experiments, mutants with a slightly different strategy are generated during reproduction at the end of each season and interference competition continually prevents their successful invasion for intermediate season duration.
evidence: This is an explanation for the evolutionary bistability

claim: Interference competition explains why the two strategies are meta-stable.
source: This explains why the two strategies are meta-stable.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of competition dynamics

claim: Evolutionary bi-stability may provide a simple explanation for the fact that many unicellular organisms do not evolve multicellularity despite possessing the necessary adhesion proteins.
source: This result may also provide a simple explanation for the fact that many unicellular organisms do not evolve multicellularity despite possessing the necessary adhesion proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the results

claim: Evolutionary bi-stability protects the multicellular strategy from evolutionary reversal to unicellularity over a large range of environmental conditions.
source: Moreover, evolutionary bi-stability protects the multicellular strategy from evolutionary reversal to unicellularity over a large range of environmental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the evolutionary bistability results

claim: Evolving multicellular organisms may incur fitness costs that are not present at the unicellular level.
source: However, evolving multicellular organisms may incur fitness costs that are not present at the unicellular level (Rebolleda-Gómez and Travisano, 2018; Rainey and Rainey, 2003; Ratcliff et al., 2012; Yokota and Sterner, 2011; Kapsetaki and West, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Undifferentiated multicellularity can evolve in a cell-based model as a byproduct of an emergent collective integration of spatial cues.
source: We demonstrated that undifferentiated multicellularity can evolve in a cell-based model as a byproduct of an emergent collective integration of spatial cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study

claim: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by reducing the death rate of cells in a cluster.
source: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by reducing the death rate of cells in a cluster (Staps et al., 2019; Pichugin et al., 2017), through social interaction (Garcia and De Monte, 2013; Joshi et al., 2017), by incorporating trade-offs between fitness and functional specialisation (Ispolatov et al., 2012), or by allowing cells to exclude non-cooperating cells (Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Staps et al., 2019 and Pichugin et al., 2017

claim: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected through social interaction.
source: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by reducing the death rate of cells in a cluster (Staps et al., 2019; Pichugin et al., 2017), through social interaction (Garcia and De Monte, 2013; Joshi et al., 2017), by incorporating trade-offs between fitness and functional specialisation (Ispolatov et al., 2012), or by allowing cells to exclude non-cooperating cells (Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garcia and De Monte, 2013 and Joshi et al., 2017

claim: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by incorporating trade-offs between fitness and functional specialisation.
source: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by reducing the death rate of cells in a cluster (Staps et al., 2019; Pichugin et al., 2017), through social interaction (Garcia and De Monte, 2013; Joshi et al., 2017), by incorporating trade-offs between fitness and functional specialisation (Ispolatov et al., 2012), or by allowing cells to exclude non-cooperating cells (Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ispolatov et al., 2012

claim: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by allowing cells to exclude non-cooperating cells.
source: Previous computational models have shown that multicellularity can be selected by reducing the death rate of cells in a cluster (Staps et al., 2019; Pichugin et al., 2017), through social interaction (Garcia and De Monte, 2013; Joshi et al., 2017), by incorporating trade-offs between fitness and functional specialisation (Ispolatov et al., 2012), or by allowing cells to exclude non-cooperating cells (Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003

claim: Earlier work found that multicellular structuring can emerge without direct selection when cells are destabilised by their internal molecular dynamics.
source: Earlier work found that multicellular structuring can emerge without direct selection when cells are destabilised by their internal molecular dynamics (e.g. the cell cycle) (Furusawa and Kaneko, 2002), or because of a toxic external environment (Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Furusawa and Kaneko, 2002

claim: Earlier work found that multicellular structuring can emerge without direct selection because of a toxic external environment.
source: Earlier work found that multicellular structuring can emerge without direct selection when cells are destabilised by their internal molecular dynamics (e.g. the cell cycle) (Furusawa and Kaneko, 2002), or because of a toxic external environment (Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duran-Nebreda et al., 2016

claim: In previous models where multicellular structuring emerges without direct selection, cell differentiation stabilises cell growth and arises as a consequence of physiological or metabolic trade-offs.
source: In both cases, cell differentiation stabilises cell growth and arises as a consequence of physiological or metabolic trade-offs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous models

claim: Division of labour is not a strict requirement for emergent aggregation.
source: With our model setup, we show that division of labour - although important - is not a strict requirement for emergent aggregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study

claim: A limitation of the current model is that cells have a narrow set of possibilities for adapting to the environment, as the only mutable traits are their ligands and receptors.
source: A limitation of the current model is that cells have a narrow set of possibilities for adapting to the environment, as the only mutable traits are their ligands and receptors.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model limitation

claim: Cells' adaptation to the environment is solely mediated by their adhesion to one another in the current model.
source: Therefore, their adaptation to the environment is solely mediated by their adhesion to one another and selection for multicellularity can only occur because adhering clusters always perform chemotaxis better than individual cells.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model design

claim: Selection for multicellularity can only occur because adhering clusters always perform chemotaxis better than individual cells.
source: Therefore, their adaptation to the environment is solely mediated by their adhesion to one another and selection for multicellularity can only occur because adhering clusters always perform chemotaxis better than individual cells.
